record.summary: Lakshmi Reddy (68) died 14 months ago, leaving a house and a small agricultural plot. Two weeks before her death, a one‑page typed will dated 9 days before her death was signed in her favour, bequeathing the property to her son Suresh. The will was witnessed by the hospital administrative clerk and Suresh's friend, and was not registered. Hospital records show Lakshmi was admitted for kidney failure, receiving sedatives, and was noted as "intermittently confused, oriented to person only" the day before the will. An unwitnessed handwritten note from 6 years ago states the three children should share equally. Suresh has begun mutation of the property and listed the land for sale. Anita and Kiran, the other children, learned of the will after the funeral and wish to contest it and stop the sale.
record.goal: Anita and Kiran want to know if they can contest the will, stop the sale of the land immediately, and understand their realistic chances.
questions: Do you have any medical records or doctor’s notes confirming Lakshmi's mental capacity on the day the will was signed?
Can you provide the full names, addresses, and contact details of the two witnesses to the will?
Has any other will or testament (registered or unregistered) been made by Lakshmi besides the handwritten note?
Have you or your siblings sent any legal notice to Suresh or the buyer to halt the sale of the land?
In which state or jurisdiction is the house and agricultural land located?
contradictions: The story says the will was signed "two weeks before her death," while the evidence states the will is dated "9 days before Lakshmi's death" – a discrepancy of about five days.
evidence:
The will is a typed one-page document dated 9 days before Lakshmi's death, signed with a shaky signature and witnessed by two people: the hospital's administrative clerk and Suresh's friend. It was not registered. Hospital records show Lakshmi was admitted for kidney failure and was receiving sedatives and pain medication, and a nursing note from the day before the will records her as "intermittently confused, oriented to person only." There is no doctor's certificate of capacity on the day of signing.

An earlier handwritten note from 6 years ago, found by Anita in a family album, says "all three children should share equally," but it is unwitnessed and unsigned beyond initials. Suresh's bank statements show he paid most of the hospital bills, which supports his caregiving claim. A cousin states that Suresh asked Lakshmi to "sign something" in hospital and she "didn't seem to know what it was," but the cousin was not present for the signing. The property listing for the land is already live online, and the municipal record shows Suresh's mutation application filed three weeks ago, still pending.
